cargo: Unsecured liabilities amount to £910 1s. 11d. The assets are returned at £97, thus leaving a deficiency of £815 1s. 11d. The receiving order was made on the 17th ult., on the petition of the creditor, an order of adjudication has since been made. The bankrupt states that he commenced business in 1884 with £100 capital, in his own name, and that he continued that business until July 31st last. The bankrupt also states that on that date a meeting of his creditors was held, and subsequently he executed a deed of assignment, a Mr. Woolf being the trustee. The bankrupt alleges his failure has been caused through loss through death of horses, bad debts, and law expenses. The bankrupt further states that all his assets have been handed over to Mr. Woolf, the trustee, under the deed of assignment. I have not yet been able to obtain from Mr. Woolf any accounts and particulars. Mr. Woolf also has the books.

Hitherto it has been the practice for a proposed rise to take effect immediately, and the result is frequently awkward, to say the least of it, for the manufacturer who has much as he may have quoted a certain sum for a monument to a customer, and may find the raw material immediately afterwards enhanced in price. raw_line: Against this the defenders appealed to the Sheriff-Principal, who has now given judgment. His lordship opens up the record, allows the pursuer to amend his pleadings, and, this having been done, closes the record of new, reserving the question of expenses. His lordship finds that on a true construction of the charter-party the sum of £20 provided therein as liquidated damages for a breach of the stipulation that the ship should be addressed “for inward reporting to charterers' agents at port of discharge, paying usual commission,” was to be treated as ascertained damages payable in the event of a breach of that stipulation, and was not subject to the modification as a penalty, on evidence as to the amount of damage.
His lordship remits to the Sheriff-Substitute for further procedure.

cargo: This bankrupt appeared for his public examination at the Walsall Bankruptcy Court on Friday last, before the Registrar. The statement of affairs filed by the debtor disclosed gross liabilities amounting to £649 19s. 8d., of which £579 0s. 9d. was expected to rank against the estate for dividend. The assets, after deducting £70 19s. for the claims of preferential creditors payable in full, were returned at £27 10s. 8d., thus leaving a deficiency of £551 10s. The debtor in the course of his examination by the Official Receiver stated that he was in a situation until 1868, when he commenced business in Ward Street, Walsall, and in May, 1884, he bought a business and plant in High Street, Bloxwich, for £50, where he afterwards went to reside. He alleged his failure to have been caused through bad trade, bad debts, and pressure by creditors. The examination was ordered to be closed.

cargo: The public examination has been held at Exeter. The Official Receiver said there was no physical inability in Mr. E. T. Scammell to prevent him from attending the Court, he (the Official Receiver) thought he should have been there. The statement which he sent in a declared statement of affairs was a very long account, and he (the Official Receiver) did not think it was necessary. He said it was his health, and secondly his reason for going away was to see his principal creditor, Mr. Stephens. After seeing him, he came to the conclusion that it would be more convenient to reside further up the country, and he went with his uncle led to his taking part in some gold enterprise. This was making from £400 to £500. This foreshadowed some kind of dividend to the creditors, which he (the Official Receiver) hoped would be realised. Mr. Scammell thought it his primary duty to be making money fast, in the interests of his creditors, to stay in Australia.-The examination was adjourned.
